Key_Finding: The RiTe model identifies five integrated domains (Evidence, Technology, Users, Team, Organization) that collectively determine successful implementation of digital rehabilitation technologies in NHS settings.
U_Examples: Digital literacy; service-user beliefs about benefit; staff willingness to use; training and skills; social support for engagement
T_Examples: Ease of use; technology features and suitability; physical environment and connectivity; hardware requirements; user interface clarity
I_Examples: Funding and procurement processes; policy compliance (information governance, clinical safety); regulatory requirements; institutional support structures
O_Examples: Organizational leadership and resource planning; change management; collaboration between teams; technology provider support; learning from other implementations

Title: Nurses' Perspective of Barrier Structure and Promotion Strategies for Digital Health Transformation: An Interpretive Structural Modeling Approach.
Primary_Determinants: Organizational culture; Stakeholder collaboration; Nursing acceptance; Infrastructure readiness; Policy alignment
Key_Finding: Organizational culture of nursing plays a fundamental role in digital health transformation, with multilayered barriers requiring coordination across clinical, developmental, and policy levels.
U_Examples: Nursing perspective; staff acceptance; organizational culture
T_Examples: Infrastructure readiness; system reliability
I_Examples: Policy levels; regulatory alignment
O_Examples: Stakeholder collaboration; change management; leadership coordination

Title: New eHealth Users After COVID-19: Adoption and Resistance in Spain.
Primary_Determinants: Age (>65 years as barrier); Digital device use frequency; Education level; Geographic location (rural vs urban); Gender
Key_Finding: eHealth access in Spain increased from 50.2% to 85.4% (2018–2025), with age emerging as the primary barrier in 2025 while frequent digital device use became a key enabler, despite persistent digital divides in older and less-educated populations.
U_Examples: Digital literacy; older adults' concerns about reduced human interaction; gender differences in technological confidence; user empowerment and self-management; perceived usefulness during pandemic necessity
T_Examples: Mobile application adoption (24.4% to 80.2%); smartphone proliferation as entry point; technological competence; digital infrastructure; mHealth platforms
I_Examples: Universal healthcare system with decentralized regional subsystems; General Health Law equity principle; pandemic as systemic shock accelerating digitalization; digital inclusion policy needs; health equity in 21st century redefined to include digital access rights

Title: Design and Implementation of a State-Wide Network for Near Real-Time Public Health Surveillance and Research: The Minnesota Electronic Health Record Consortium Experience.
Primary_Determinants: Federated data architecture; governance structure and consensus-based decision-making; data standardization and harmonization (OMOP model); funding and sustained resource commitment; multi-stakeholder collaboration and partnerships
Key_Finding: MNEHRC successfully implemented a state-wide EHR consortium serving >90% of Minnesota's population through federated data governance, technical standardization, and institutional alignment with public health agencies and health systems.
T_Examples: OMOP common data model; privacy-preserving record linkage; secure hash algorithm; federated architecture; data quality assessment tools; standardized mappings across Epic systems
I_Examples: Governance model with voting members; data use agreements; funding from MDH and CDC; collaboration with state vital statistics, immunization registries, Medicaid; public health surveillance mandate
O_Examples: Executive Committee for day-to-day operations; Administrative Core for coordination and contracts; Technical Assistance Core for data management; 2-year implementation timeline; project-specific appendices and contracting processes

Title: Interoperability Barriers in the European Health Data Space: A Scoping Review.
Venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
Primary_Determinants: Technical standardization gaps (HL7 FHIR, OMOP adoption); semantic and organizational interoperability barriers; national implementation disparities; legal and regulatory alignment; metadata catalogue absence
Key_Finding: EHDS implementation is hindered by persistent technical, organizational, and legal barriers despite regulatory frameworks, with Member States showing inconsistent adoption of interoperability standards.
T_Examples: HL7 FHIR adoption variability; OMOP implementation inconsistency; EEHRxF standardization; semantic gaps; metadata catalogue deficiency
I_Examples: Regulatory frameworks; legal dimension barriers; Member State coordination gaps; European Health Data Space regulation scope
O_Examples: National implementation disparities; organizational gaps; Member State coordination requirements; standardization strategy prioritization

Title: Exploring Factors Associated With the Stalled Implementation of a Ground-Up Electronic Health Record System in South Africa: Qualitative Insights From the E-Tick Case Study Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR).
Primary_Determinants: Outer setting factors (funding cuts, political appointments, governance gaps); user engagement and co-design; provincial health department capacity and support; policy alignment; corruption and tender system mismanagement
Key_Finding: E-tick implementation stalled despite strong user adoption and co-design due to critical outer setting factors including funding withdrawal, governance instability, and lack of provincial-level institutional support stemming from corruption and capacity gaps.
U_Examples: User adoption; clinician co-design; end-user engagement; iterative development with manager and clinician input
T_Examples: System design for data quality improvement; integration with existing provincial reporting systems; expandability to include diagnosis and lab results
I_Examples: National Digital Health Strategy alignment; provincial health department capacity gaps; political appointments; policy direction; tender system corruption and mistrust
O_Examples: Change of developers; funding cuts; provincial leadership support withdrawal; resistance to leveraging locally-developed systems; top-down versus bottom-up process synergy

Title: A Complex Digital Health Intervention to Support People With HIV: Organizational Readiness Survey Study and Preimplementation Planning for a Hybrid Effectiveness-Implementation Study.
Primary_Determinants: Organizational readiness for change; Provider baseline digital health tool experience; Implementation strategy specification; Framework alignment (RE-AIM, CFIR); Multisite coordination and real-world context adaptation
Key_Finding: Prospective hybrid trial planning for complex DHI implementation requires proactive integration of implementation science frameworks and readiness assessment to balance generalizability with internal validity, with organizational readiness scores and provider digital literacy as key preimplementation determinants.
U_Examples: Provider baseline mHealth tool usage; Digital literacy and familiarity with patient-facing components; Organizational readiness commitment and efficacy (ORIC scores: physicians 48.0 vs research assistants 52.5)
T_Examples: Multifeature smartphone app architecture; Backend paradata and usage data capture; System interoperability within clinic-embedded context; Integration with existing HIV care workflows
I_Examples: Alignment with DC Cohort Study infrastructure; Ethics review and IRB approval; Mapping to national HIV care guidelines; Hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial design (type II)
O_Examples: 18-month preimplementation planning phase; Interdisciplinary team (clinical psychology, program evaluation, implementation research); Iterative framework integration (RE-AIM, CFIR); Implementation strategy step specification; Research assistant role as de facto site implementation leads; Change management and fidelity measurement planning

Title: Health Care Worker Perspectives After New Electronic Health Record Implementation in an Oncology Ambulatory Clinic: Qualitative and Quality-Improvement Insights.
Primary_Determinants: Staff training and preparedness; Workflow integration and system usability; Organizational change management and QI response; Clinical communication and safety systems; Peer support and role-specific design
Key_Finding: EHR implementation in ambulatory oncology revealed that staff acceptance and effectiveness depend on comprehensive training, workflow optimization, multidisciplinary change management, and institutional responsiveness to identified safety and efficiency challenges.
U_Examples: Limited training; cognitive overload; peer support; burnout; role-specific needs
T_Examples: Navigation complexity; system integration; multiple programs; imaging delays; order duplication
I_Examples: Regional connectivity; multidisciplinary governance; QI initiatives; institutional responsiveness
O_Examples: Education rounds; working groups; role-specific training; workflow optimization; AI integration

Title: The Regional Implementation of an Electronic Health Record-Integrated Ambient Scribe in Primary and Secondary Care in England: Real-Time Qualitative Evaluation.
Primary_Determinants: Workflow integration challenges; clinician adaptation to technology; stand-alone vs integrated system design; organizational readiness for standardization; documentation quality and safety concerns
Key_Finding: Integration pathways present distinct trade-offs: stand-alone systems are easier to adopt but offer limited long-term benefits, while integrated systems require greater effort and standardization yet promise improved efficiency and safety.
U_Examples: Clinician adjustment of speech patterns; patient-clinician interaction quality; technology confidence and openness; note editing burden; workflow fit across primary and secondary care
T_Examples: EHR integration pathways; template validation across settings; automated note accuracy; system flexibility and interoperability; documentation errors (hallucinations, omissions)
I_Examples: Regulatory oversight needs; procurement strategy alignment; strategic uncertainty in immature market; risk-benefit assessment for health systems
O_Examples: Change management across diverse settings; leadership and project governance; implementation phasing and timeline; organizational standardization requirements; vendor relationship management

Title: Challenges and facilitators of electronic health record implementation: a scoping review.
Primary_Determinants: Leadership and political support; Infrastructure investment; Stakeholder engagement; Adherence to standards (HL7/FHIR/ICD-10); Comprehensive training programs
Key_Finding: EHR implementation success depends on multilevel factors spanning governance, policy, leadership, human resources, infrastructure, and interoperability rather than technology alone.
U_Examples: Comprehensive training programs; stakeholder engagement; skilled personnel
T_Examples: Interoperability issues; infrastructure limitations; standards adherence (ICD-10)
I_Examples: Lack of clear policies; weak strategic oversight; governance challenges; policy recommendations; national roadmaps; sustainable funding
O_Examples: Strong leadership and political support; operational guidelines; multi-level collaboration; change management

Title: Adoption, digital health literacy, and patient satisfaction of Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission: an analytical cross-sectional study among outpatient department attendees.
Primary_Determinants: Digital health literacy; Data privacy concerns; Language barriers; Economic constraints (data plan costs); Preference for in-person healthcare
Key_Finding: ABDM adoption remains limited despite operational efficiency, with significant barriers related to digital literacy, privacy concerns, economic constraints, and substantial disparities across gender, age, and education levels.
U_Examples: 88% needed training and support; 65.6% difficulty using health apps; 64.0% language difficulties; 58.6% lacked ABDM knowledge despite facility participation; gender, age, educational disparities in digital literacy
T_Examples: 81.9% barrier: high data plan costs; technical errors; poor internet connectivity; difficulty understanding digital procedures
I_Examples: Integration with AB-PMJAY scheme; government tertiary care facility implementation; national digital health policy alignment
O_Examples: Limited ABHA registration adoption vs. conventional OPD; need for on-site trained facilitators; multilingual interface simplification; community-based digital literacy programs recommended

Title: When Tech Meets Touch: Multistakeholder Perspectives and Implementation Strategies for eHealth in Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review Using Computational Linguistics.
Primary_Determinants: Stakeholder sentiment and emotional responses; workflow integration and usability; organizational change management; institutional policies and incentives; technical interoperability and infrastructure
Key_Finding: A hybrid computational-qualitative systematic review mapping implementation barriers and facilitators of digital health interventions in CKD management to CFIR domains and ERIC strategies, with sentiment analysis quantifying affective dimensions of stakeholder acceptance.
U_Examples: Clinician acceptance; stakeholder emotional responses; digital literacy; workflow fit; patient empowerment and engagement
T_Examples: System interoperability; technical barriers; infrastructure reliability; data exchange standards; remote monitoring and telehealth platforms
I_Examples: Healthcare policies; regulatory frameworks; funding mandates; institutional governance; incentives for adoption
O_Examples: Change management strategies; leadership support; implementation strategy selection via ERIC; project management; resource allocation

Title: Exploring the Dynamics of Actors, Structural Factors, and Bricolage in the Implementation and Sustainability of eHealth Solutions: Qualitative Multiple-Case Study.
Primary_Determinants: Actor roles and bricolage capacity; Structural enablers (colocation, supportive management, stable teams, superusers, tailored training); Organizational barriers (silos, leadership shifts, staffing shortages, geographic dispersion); Contextual knowledge and dual expertise
Key_Finding: Actors become effective bricoleurs when assigned roles, contextual knowledge, and backstage access enable improvisation in response to unforeseen implementation challenges, with structural conditions either expanding or constraining this adaptive capacity.
U_Examples: Superusers, tailored training, follow-up support activities, informal evaluations, staff acceptance of innovation roles
T_Examples: eHealth solution complexity perceived as challenging, technical infrastructure, integration with existing systems
I_Examples: Policy mandates for eHealth adoption, organizational governance, cross-sectoral collaboration frameworks, regional digitalization strategy alignment
O_Examples: Colocation, supportive management, stable teams, leadership involvement, project management, staffing stability, organizational silos as barriers, high turnover constraints

Title: Shoulder-to-shoulder: healthcare professionals' experiences of learning during electronic health record implementation in municipal primary care.
Venue: Scandinavian journal of primary health care
Primary_Determinants: Formal training alignment with clinical work; peer-based learning and shoulder-to-shoulder support; staffing and time constraints; digital competencies; workplace learning communities
Key_Finding: Peer-based 'shoulder-to-shoulder' learning embedded in everyday work emerged as an adaptive practice essential to EHR implementation success, complementing and sometimes compensating for inadequate formal training in municipal primary care.
U_Examples: Digital competencies; formal training poorly aligned with work; peer support; mutual learning; problem-solving collaboration
T_Examples: System usability; workflow integration; documentation practices; information flow standardization
I_Examples: Regional rollout strategy; Health Platform implementation policy; municipal healthcare structure; training program design by Helseplattformen AS
O_Examples: Leadership support; change management; superuser support structure; staffing levels; resource constraints; implementation coordinator role; department manager involvement

Title: Feasibility and Implementation of an eHealth Dashboard for the Remote Monitoring of Dutch Patients With Chronic Myeloid Leukemia: Multimethods Approach.
Primary_Determinants: Data integration with EMR; user adoption by patients; workflow integration; data completeness and reliability; perceived added value versus existing systems
Key_Finding: Remote monitoring dashboard for CML shows promise but requires automated EMR integration, improved data completeness, and better clinical workflow alignment before large-scale implementation.
U_Examples: Limited patient app adoption; lack of perceived added value; need for enhanced user training and preparation support
T_Examples: Lack of EMR integration; manual data entry limitations; absence of automated lab data exchange except one hospital; HL7/FHIR interoperability standards being upgraded; additional login procedures required
I_Examples: Protocol-based care delivery across dispersed facilities; Dutch guidelines for BCR::ABL1 monitoring; regulatory compliance (GDPR, NEN7510); evidence-based CML guideline alignment
O_Examples: HCP involvement in design-thinking development; convenience sampling of 8 HCPs from university and general hospitals; leadership introduction of dashboard; change management through CMyLife team support

Title: Nurses' Work Satisfaction With Electronic Medical Record Use and Associated Facilitators and Barriers in Palestine.
Primary_Determinants: Ease of system use; EMR training; Technical support satisfaction; Age; User-friendliness perception
Key_Finding: Nurses in Palestinian governmental hospitals reported moderate satisfaction (52.1%) with EMR use, with ease of use, training, technical support, and age as significant predictors explaining 23.4% of variance in work satisfaction.
U_Examples: Ease of system navigation; User-friendliness perception; EMR training received; Fear of system disrupting work patterns; Digital literacy concerns
T_Examples: System complexity; Technical support satisfaction; Computer availability; System crashes; System reliability and performance
I_Examples: Healthcare sector challenges from political and financial instability in Palestine; Lack of resources; Staffing shortages; Infrastructure constraints
O_Examples: EMR training provision; Technical support availability; Change management during EMR implementation; Workload and documentation time allocation

Title: Assessment of the use of electronic medical records system and barriers in Rwanda.
Venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
Primary_Determinants: Infrastructure (electricity, internet); Training and user guides; System reliability and maintenance; Staff capacity and digital literacy; Organizational readiness and resources
Key_Finding: District hospitals in Rwanda achieved high EMR adoption (100%), while health centers showed lower utilization (33%), with barriers including infrastructure deficits, inadequate training, system damage, and lack of technical support.
U_Examples: Limited training on EMR use; lack of user guides; staff shortages; preferences for EMRs over paper-based methods; varied digital literacy levels
T_Examples: Internet connectivity challenges; power disruptions; system damage and corrupted files; software glitches; server timeouts; limited computer access
I_Examples: Government support for OpenMRS adoption; policy framework for EMR implementation across health system levels; national ethics committee oversight
O_Examples: Facility-level EMR implementation strategies; leadership engagement with health facility representatives; resource allocation for infrastructure updates; system diversity across facilities

Title: Incorporating human factors methods into the configuration and implementation of an electronic health record system.
Primary_Determinants: Usability evaluation and human factors integration; Clinical workflow alignment; End-user engagement; Project timeline and resource allocation; Safety optimization
Key_Finding: Systematic incorporation of human factors methods throughout a 7-year EHR implementation identified over 2,000 usability improvements and ensured safety and workflow alignment, though requiring dedicated time and resources in project planning.
U_Examples: Usability evaluations with 400+ clinical end users; workflow fit; clinician acceptance; safety-efficiency optimization
T_Examples: EHR build configuration; technology-related safety risks; system design optimization
I_Examples: Project timeline planning; resource allocation for HF evaluation; implementation governance across 7-year rollout
O_Examples: Human factors team engagement; change management through end-user involvement; project execution strategy; phased implementation across 30 evaluations

Title: E-Health implementation in Pakistan: challenges, opportunities, and the path forward.
Primary_Determinants: Digital infrastructure gaps; workforce digital literacy and training; governance and regulatory misalignment; perceived ease of use and usefulness; stakeholder coordination and funding mechanisms
Key_Finding: E-Health adoption in Pakistan requires integrated sociotechnical transformation addressing policy-practice alignment, digital equity, and user-centered design rather than technology deployment alone.
U_Examples: Low digital literacy among healthcare providers; perceived ease of use barriers; workforce training gaps in EHR and teleconsultation systems; user-centered design deficits
T_Examples: Uneven internet connectivity in rural areas; power supply issues; lack of interoperable health information systems; infrastructure gaps limiting integration and scalability
I_Examples: National Digital Health Framework 2022–2030; fragmented governance across government/private/NGO sectors; weak regulatory frameworks and enforcement mechanisms; limited public health expenditure; data protection and AI governance concerns
O_Examples: Stakeholder misalignment between government, healthcare providers, technology partners; shortage of coordinated implementation mechanisms; isolated projects lacking systemic integration; inadequate sustained funding for E-Health initiatives

Title: ePA4all-Exploring facilitators and barriers to the adoption of the electronic health record in Germany: A study protocol for a mixed-methods analysis.
Primary_Determinants: Digital health literacy; Privacy and data protection concerns; Usability and workflow integration; Trust in data governance; Administrative burden on healthcare providers
Key_Finding: The study protocol aims to identify structural, organizational, and individual determinants of ePA adoption across patient and healthcare provider perspectives using CFIR framework to inform strategies for successful implementation of Germany's opt-out national electronic health record system.
U_Examples: Digital health literacy; Privacy concerns; Trust in data security; Perceived value and convenience; Patient empowerment and engagement
T_Examples: System interoperability; Telematics infrastructure; Data exchange standards; Usability and interface design; Integration with practice information systems
I_Examples: Opt-out policy mandate; Legal obligations for document upload; Data governance and transparency frameworks; Regulatory requirements; Health insurance coordination
O_Examples: Administrative burden on practices; Workflow integration challenges; Documentation time and cognitive load; Staff training and patient education; Change management strategies
